title: Do street dogs understand when we point?
blurb: Scientists from IISER Kolkata pointed at one of two covered bowls for over 200 street dogs. Most puppies followed the finger, but grown dogs were more careful.

original.title: Free-ranging dogs show age related plasticity in their ability to follow human pointing
original.authors: Bhattacharjee, D., Nikhil Dev, N., Gupta, S., and others, with Bhadra, A.

cards.b: Pet dogs are good at following a pointing finger to find food. But pet dogs live with people and are trained. India has millions of street dogs who find their own food. People can be friends to them, or a danger. Do street dogs understand pointing too, and does it change as they grow up?

Anindita Bhadra leads a lab at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, IISER Kolkata, in West Bengal, that studies street dogs. Debottam Bhattacharjee was the first author of the study. Nikhil Dev, Shreya Gupta, Shubhra Sau, Rohan Sarkar, Arpita Biswas, Arunita Banerjee, Daisy Babu and Diksha Mehta also took part. They published in 2017.

The team tested 68 puppies, 58 young dogs and 83 grown dogs, in markets, railway stations and streets of two towns in West Bengal. One scientist hid a piece of raw chicken under the cardboard lid of one of two bowls. Both bowls smelled of chicken, so smell could not help. A second scientist, who did not know which bowl had food, pointed at one. Each dog was tried three times in a row.

img.alt: A white and black street dog sniffing the edge of a road in Hyderabad.
img.credit: Raja Sekhar Chimirala, CC BY 4.0, via iNaturalist

cards.b: Almost 9 in 10 puppies came to the bowls, and most of them followed the pointing finger. Fewer young and grown dogs came close. Of those that did, about half followed the point. Young dogs looked back and forth between the person and the bowls the most. Only grown dogs learned from the three tries. If they followed the point and found chicken, they followed again. If they followed and found none, they stopped.

img.alt: A bar graph comparing puppies, young dogs and grown dogs. More puppies followed the pointing than the older dogs.
img.credit: Figure 1, Bhattacharjee et al., PLOS ONE 2017, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Over 200 dogs took part, which is a lot for a study like this. But all were from one part of West Bengal. The dogs were free to walk away, so many never came near the bowls. That makes testing harder. Scientists think puppies are born ready to follow people, and older dogs learn to be careful.

Street dogs live closely with people, without being anyone's pet. Understanding how they think helps people and dogs live together safely. It also shows that following a human point does not need training. Puppies can do it, and grown dogs use what life has taught them about whether people can be trusted.

Test a dog the way the scientists did. Put two upturned cups on the floor, with a treat under one. Call the dog, then point at the cup with the treat, without touching it. Does the dog go to that cup? Try five times, hiding the treat under a different cup each time. Count how often the dog follows your point.
cards.note: Only try this with a friendly dog you know, with a grown-up beside you.

cards.b: Puppies trusted the pointing person easily, but grown dogs were more careful. Is it better to trust everyone, or to be careful until you know someone? Think of a time you trusted someone new. What helped you decide?

words.m: a dog that lives freely on the streets and finds their own food
a signal, like a pointed finger, that shows where to look
looking back and forth between a person and a thing
believing that someone will not trick or hurt you
